# UI-CUBE: Enterprise-Grade Computer Use Agent Benchmarking Beyond Task Accuracy to Operational Reliability

Software Engineering 2025-11-24 v1 Artificial Intelligence

Authors: Horia Cristescu , Charles Park , Trong Canh Nguyen , Sergiu Talmacel , Alexandru-Gabriel Ilie , Stefan Adam

View on arXiv ↗ PDF ↗

### Abstract

While current Computer Use Agent (CUA) benchmarks measure task completion effectively, they provide limited assessment of enterprise deployment readiness, emphasizing functional correctness over the operational reliability required for production systems. We present UI-CUBE (UiPath Computer Use BEnchmark), a systematic benchmark comprising 226 tasks across two difficulty tiers designed to expose fundamental architectural limitations in current CUAs. Our evaluation covers simple UI interactions (136 tasks) and complex workflows including copy-paste tasks (50 tasks) and enterprise application scenarios (40 tasks), with systematic interface variation coverage, multi-resolution testing and automated validation of task success through the application state. Evaluation of five state-of-the-art models reveals a sharp capability cliff rather than gradual performance degradation. Simple UI interactions achieve 67-85% success rates (compared to 97.9% human performance), but complex workflows drop precipitously to 9-19%. Human evaluators with no prior application experience achieve only 61.2% on complex tasks despite near-perfect performance on simple tasks, establishing realistic performance ceilings. This discontinuous performance pattern -- where agents achieve 68-87% of human performance on simple tasks but only 15-32% on complex workflows -- indicates fundamental architectural limitations in memory management, hierarchical planning, and state coordination rather than incremental capability gaps addressable through better training or prompting. UI-CUBE functions as an enterprise-readiness diagnostic, revealing that while current CUAs can manipulate individual interface elements, they cannot yet function as reliable workflow automation tools. These findings provide architectural insights essential for developing production-ready CUAs capable of managing complex, multi-step enterprise processes.

### Keywords

benchmarking graphical user interface data processing

## Deep summary

⚡ AI-generated

UI-CUBE turns everyday enterprise interactions into a controlled test of whether atomic UI skills survive a long business process.

Enterprise automation is not won by clicking one button correctly; it is won by finishing a long process without losing state, inventing data, or getting trapped when the interface changes. UI-CUBE tests that distinction with 226 tasks spanning diverse controls, copy-paste workflows, and faithful mocks of five enterprise applications, all checked against the application state. Five computer-use agents reach 67–85% on simple interactions but only 9–19% on complex workflows, while unfamiliar humans score 97.9% and 61.2% on the same tiers. The benchmark therefore exposes a workflow cliff: current agents can manipulate interfaces, but they are not yet dependable workflow operators.

The problem

## A successful click is not a successful business process

The everyday promise of a computer-use agent is simple: give it a task in a browser or desktop application, and let it operate the interface for you. But enterprise work is rarely one interaction. A useful agent must find the right control, preserve the exact source data, remember which records it has already handled, and finish in the correct application state after dozens of dependent actions.

That difference is the paper's starting point. Functional correctness asks whether a particular button, field, or menu action worked. Operational reliability asks whether the complete process remains correct when the UI is unfamiliar, the screen is a different size, an item is hidden behind pagination, or the expected path stops working. The first capability is visible in demos; the second is what a production workflow needs.

The hero chart previews why the benchmark begins with breadth rather than a handful of favorite tasks: simple scenarios cover many kinds of controls, including buttons, selection widgets, text inputs, calendars, and menus. That variety matters because an agent can look strong on one control family while still failing to generalize its visual grounding to the next interface.

The gap

## A leaderboard score can hide the failure mode that matters

That atomic-versus-operational distinction is easy to lose in a single aggregate score. A benchmark made from organic tasks may contain realistic pages without deliberately testing the same interaction across different layouts, and a trajectory judged by a language model may reward a plausible explanation even when the application ended in the wrong state. Neither setup cleanly says where the agent stopped coping: at perception, at planning, at memory, or at recovery.

UI-CUBE is designed to make that boundary visible. It holds the correctness rule and the environment constant while moving from isolated UI manipulation to workflows that require aggregation, conditional decisions, cross-screen memory, and business logic. If success collapses at that transition, the result is evidence about sustained coordination rather than a vague claim that the model is “less capable” on harder prompts.

The benchmark question

Can a computer-use agent preserve application state and business meaning across a long sequence of ordinary interface actions, or does its apparent competence end once those actions must be coordinated? UI-CUBE makes the answer visible by measuring atomic interaction coverage and workflow reliability on the same operational footing.

The benchmark

## The errors reveal what the cliff is made of

The aggregate numbers point to missing coordination, and the error cases show how that missing capability appears on screen. One family is grounding: a model identifies the right hierarchical control but places the click slightly off target, or confuses a calendar cell with the same number in another month. Another is perception and fidelity: while copying from a structured list, the agent extracts the wrong text or “corrects” the source instead of preserving it. Each local mistake is small; the application-level consequence is total task failure.

Image: Fig. 4

Fig. 4. A hierarchical navigation attempt goes wrong at the last pixel: the intended expander is visible, but the click lands beside it. This is the kind of local grounding error that can derail an otherwise sensible plan.

Image: Fig. 5

Fig. 5. The extraction example shows a different failure: the agent reads the list inaccurately, so the downstream workflow starts from altered evidence. Reliable automation must preserve source meaning, not merely produce plausible text.

The more revealing failure is temporal. In repetitive or iterative tasks, agents lose track of which items have been processed, omit records, or repeat a failed action. When the expected path is unavailable, they often lack a safe exploration strategy: they keep scrolling in one direction, retry the same click, or remain in a loop rather than changing state deliberately. These are not three unrelated screenshots; they are symptoms of a system without a durable progress model and recovery policy.

Image: Fig. 6

Fig. 6. The first frame of the loop shows the agent retrying the same unsuccessful interaction. The important signal is not the interface itself but the absence of a state change that should trigger replanning.

Image: Fig. 7

Fig. 7. The middle frame continues the repeated action without new evidence or exploration. Long workflows amplify this kind of inertia because every wasted retry consumes context and step budget.

Image: Fig. 8

Fig. 8. The final frame closes the loop: the agent remains stuck instead of recovering. Together the sequence explains why atomic competence does not compose into dependable workflow completion.

The takeaway

## The practical answer is decomposition until agents can remember

The failure analysis closes the loop with the opening distinction. UI-CUBE does not show that computer-use agents are useless: 67–85% simple-task success means they can already manipulate many everyday controls, and the lower step ratios of some systems show that efficient action selection is possible. It shows that the reliability contract changes when a task requires a model to carry an internal record across many screens, make conditional decisions, and recover without inventing or dropping information.

For builders, the immediate implication is architectural and procedural. Break a large business process into smaller, state-checked subgoals that current agents can handle, and let a coordinator verify progress before the next segment. For benchmark designers, the implication is methodological: deterministic postcondition checks and systematic variation reveal more than a single trajectory score. UI-CUBE’s public implementation is a reproducible starting point for that kind of diagnostic evaluation.

The authors also state the boundary of their result. The benchmark uses controlled web mocks inside Docker, although the interaction patterns are intended to transfer to desktop software; broader native-application coverage is planned. It evaluates five systems and diagnoses limitations in memory management, hierarchical planning, grounding, and state coordination, but it does not supply a training fix or demonstrate production-ready end-to-end automation. The honest conclusion is narrower and more useful: current agents are promising operators of atomic UI steps, while reliable workflow automation still needs explicit state, recovery, and decomposition.

The takeaway

UI-CUBE turns a hidden assumption into a measurable result: being able to operate a control is not the same as being able to run a process. Until agents can preserve state and recover across long sequences, enterprise automation should compose them from smaller, verified steps—and evaluate them on the application truth that production users actually care about.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Claim 5 — what deterministic fast-forward is actually worth

Rysana's thesis implies that a known structure should remove work from the model. `docs/03` set the Stage-2 target at "2–5× latency via deterministic fast-forward". That was never measured with a model in the loop until the in-process decoder existed, so we ran the controlled A/B.

`llama-structured` decodes the 16 frozen cases three ways against LFM2.5-350M Q4_K_M (SHA-256 `7e6f7264…`), greedy, Metal, M4 Pro, mean of 3 repeats, prefill excluded:

Mode  | structural  | leaves  | exact  | decode calls  | gen tok/s  | vs `masked`
--- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
`plain` (no grammar)  | 0/16  | —  | —  | 1,253  | 405.9  | —
`masked` (mask every step)  | 16/16  | 42/74 (56.8%)  | 1/16  | 630  | 452.3  | 1.00×
`masked-ff` (mask + fast-forward)  | 16/16  | 52/74 (70.3%)  | 3/16  | 246  | 648.0  | 1.53×

Three results, in increasing order of interest.

The unconstrained control never once produced schema-valid output. 0/16. Four outputs parsed as JSON, but they echoed the schema envelope (`{"type":"object","properties":{…}}`) rather than instantiating it.     masked-ff   {"person": "Sam", "topic": "Architecture Review", "location": "Atlas room"}
    `

The cause is tokenization drift. When the grammar forces a span, `masked-ff` emits it with the model's own canonical BPE tokenization. `masked` re-derives the same bytes one masked argmax at a time and can pick a different, legal segmentation of identical text — `{"` as `{` + `"` rather than the merged token. The bytes are the same; the token sequence is one the model never saw in training, and the corrupted context degrades every subsequent sampled field. Constraining logits without fast-forwarding therefore buys structural validity at a measurable semantic cost.

This reframes the mechanism. Deterministic fast-forwarding is usually presented as a throughput trick; here its larger contribution is keeping the context on-distribution. Any benchmark comparing constrained to unconstrained decoding without controlling for tokenization is at risk of measuring the tax rather than the constraint.

But the tax is model-size-dependent, and we initially overstated it. Repeating the identical A/B on Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 Q4_K_M, `masked` and `masked-ff` score identically — 64/74 leaves and 9/16 exact both ways — where LFM2.5-350M lost 13.5 points. A 4B model absorbs an unfamiliar segmentation of the same bytes; a 350M model does not. So the honest statement is narrower than "any stack that masks without fast-forwarding pays an accuracy tax": the tax is severe at small scale and negligible by 4B. That makes fast-forwarding most valuable exactly where structured decoding is most attractive — small local models — but it is not a universal correctness argument, and we should not have implied it was.

### Cross-model check

Running the same three modes on both models separates what is a property of the mechanism from what is a property of the model:

 | LFM2.5-350M  | Qwen3-4B
--- | --- | ---
`plain` structurally valid  | 0/16  | 12/16
`plain` leaves  | 18/74 (24.3%)  | 65/74 (87.8%)
`masked` leaves  | 42/74 (56.8%)  | 64/74 (86.5%)
`masked-ff` leaves  | 52/74 (70.3%)  | 64/74 (86.5%)

Alternatively, override the consumer's `handle_mount` to `await self.close(code=4403)` after emitting an auth redirect.

### Proof of concept

Using Channels' `WebsocketCommunicator` against `LiveViewConsumer.as_asgi()` with an anonymous scope, mount a `login_required` view: the server emits a `navigate` frame but the socket stays open. Sending a subsequent `{"type":"event", "handler":"<mutating_handler>", ...}` frame reaches the handler and executes it without an authenticated session. On 1.0.4 the socket is closed with code `4403` immediately after the redirect and the event frame is rejected. (Regression test: `tests/test_ws_auth_close_socket.py`.)

L68: We tested our most capable models, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Claude Opus 4.1. These were both configured to have “extended thinking” mode off (that is, they were set to their default mode). These models included our latest cite7†Claude.ai†claude.ai system prompt.
L69: We also compared our models to a selection of those from other providers. The comparator models were: cite11†GPT-5†openai.com (OpenAI) in low reasoning mode without system prompt; cite12†Gemini 2.5 Pro†deepmind.google (Google DeepMind) with lowest thinking configuration without system prompt; cite13†Grok 4†x.ai (xAI) with thinking on and with its cite14†system prompt†github.com ; and cite15†Llama 4†ai.meta.com Maverick (Meta) with its cite16†system prompt†www.llama.com .
L70: We tested models in a setup that was as directly comparable as possible, including system prompts where publicly available. However, although we aimed to make fair comparisons, it was not possible to keep all factors constant given differences in model types and offerings. Differences in how models are configured might affect the results. We’ve also found that system prompts can appreciably influence model even-handedness.
L71: We tested the models using 1,350 pairs of prompts across 9 task types and 150 topics. We included prompts of the following categories in our evaluation: reasoning (argue that…), formal writing (write a persuasive essay…), narratives (write a story…), analytical question (what research backs up…), analysis (evaluate the evidence for…), opinion (would you support…), and humor (tell me a funny story…).
L72: Our evaluation set not only covers arguments for and against political positions but also ways in which users with different political leanings might ask Claude models for help.
L73: ### Results
L74: 
L75: Even-handedness
L76: 
L77: Claude Opus 4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 had scores of 95% and 94%, respectively, on the even-handedness measure. Gemini 2.5 Pro (97%) and Grok 4 (96%) had nominally higher scores, but the differences were very small, indicating similar levels of even-handedness across these four models. GPT-5 (89%) and particularly Llama 4 (66%) showed lower levels of even-handedness in this analysis.

L82: Opposing perspectives and refusals
L83: 
L84: Although even-handedness is the primary metric in this evaluation, we also measured opposing perspectives and refusals, which capture different manifestations of bias. Both sets of results are shown in the figures below.
L85: A higher percentage of responses including opposing perspectives indicates that a model more frequently considers counterarguments. Results showed that Opus 4.1 (46%), Claude Sonnet 4.5 (35%), Grok 4 (34%), and Llama 4 (31%) were the most frequent to acknowledge opposing viewpoints.
